title: Why Young Indians Are Spending Lakhs on Concerts and Trips, Not Gadgets
excerpt: 62% of Gen Z plan concert-led travel this year at ₹51,000 a trip — but shaky infrastructure is pushing billions in spending to Singapore and the UAE.
body:
• A January 2026 Airbnb survey found 62% of India's Gen Z plan to travel for concerts or music festivals this year; 76% visited a city for the first time specifically for a concert, spending an average ₹51,000 per event-led trip.
  • The scale is startling: at Travis Scott's Delhi concert, 100,000 tickets sold within minutes — nearly ₹100 crore spent on a single cultural moment, per Loest Road Advisors.
  • But a Bhavan's College study finds infrastructure gaps — limited venues, surge pricing, logistics bottlenecks — are pushing young Indians toward Singapore and the UAE instead, where concert hotel rates have surged up to 300%.
  • What this means for you: if you're planning a India trip around a concert or festival this winter, book early — and if you're diaspora Gen Z, the data says you're not alone: 40%+ of young Indian travelers would cross borders for the right music event.

India's young are buying memories, not machines. A generation that watched its parents save for scooters and gold is now routing a fifth to two-fifths of its monthly income into concert tickets, weekend getaways and music-led trips — and the numbers behind the shift are hard to dismiss as a fad. The question is no longer whether the experience economy is real in India, but whether India's infrastructure can keep the spending at home.

The concert as a travel product

The anchor data comes from Airbnb's January 2026 survey: 62% of India's Gen Z plan to travel for concerts or music festivals in 2026, 76% have visited a city for the first time specifically for a concert or festival, 53% extend their stays beyond the concert dates, and the average event-led trip costs ₹51,000. Travelers are willing to allocate 21–40% of monthly income to music-led trips; 70% attend in groups.

The spending is budgeted, not impulsive. SalarySe data shows more than 70% of its 5.2 lakh salaried Gen Z users' monthly spending goes to everyday needs — the "fun fund" for concerts, travel and workshops is a deliberate line item. As VIT Vellore graduate Dhruv Jaipuria told Outlook Money: "Possessions feel like a burden, whereas experiences help us feel liberated."

"Possessions feel like a burden, whereas experiences help us feel liberated."

— Dhruv Jaipuria, VIT Vellore graduate

₹100 crore in minutes

Loest Road Advisors puts the macro frame on it: 78% of Indian consumers would rather spend on experiences than products, and 45% prefer meaningful real-world activities over scrolling. The Travis Scott Delhi concert is the exhibit: 100,000 tickets gone within minutes, nearly ₹100 crore spent on a single cultural moment. Travel spending has doubled in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, per Saptashwa TV — affordable flights, better highways, expanded rail and cheap accommodation meeting social-media-driven discovery of hidden gems, adventure sports and food trails.

The leak: outbound arbitrage

Here is the uncomfortable part. A February 2026 study by Bhavan's College's MSEED, led by Dean Dr Jateen Rajput, found that infrastructure gaps — limited venue capacity, surge pricing, logistics bottlenecks — are driving "outbound arbitrage": young Indians choosing Singapore or the UAE over Indian cities for big concerts. UAE concert hotel rates have surged up to 300%, and international destinations are winning on smoother visas, predictable pricing and purpose-built venues, Devdiscourse reported. The irony: India's experience boom is subsidizing other countries' hospitality industries.

What it means for the diaspora

For diaspora families, the trend reframes the India trip. The classic visit-home itinerary — relatives, temples, weddings — is being joined by a concert-and-getaway layer, and the winter festival calendar (Diwali through New Year) is peak season. More than 40% of young Indian travelers say they would travel internationally for music events, with the US (48%), Asia (46%) and Europe (45%) as top draws — which means diaspora Gen Z in New Jersey or the Bay Area are part of the same market, flying to see the same artists.

The actionable read: India's live-events pipeline is now a legitimate travel-planning input. If a winter India trip coincides with a major concert or festival, the data says build the itinerary around it — book early, expect surge pricing near venues, and consider that the venue-city stay, not the flight, is where the money goes. The experience economy is no longer a lifestyle footnote; at ₹51,000 a trip and rising, it is a line item in how young India — and young diaspora India — spends.
